topic: Paul Ekman & Wallace Friesen (1969-1978): Frame-by-Frame Microexpressions, FACS & the 'Pinocchio Nose' Myth
visual_mode_reason: Slow-motion 16mm film inspection of a 1/15-second facial flash is a classic visual detective scene, grounded in subcortical amygdala motor pathways outrunning voluntary cortical masking.

primary_case.title: Paul Ekman & Wallace Friesen's slow-motion clinical film leakage discovery & Facial Action Coding System (FACS)
primary_case.place: Langley Porter Neuropsychiatric Institute, UC San Francisco

people.name: Paul Ekman
people.role: UCSF psychologist who discovered brief involuntary microexpressions on slow-motion interview film while also warning that no facial tic guarantees lying

people.name: Wallace V. Friesen
people.role: Collaborator who co-discovered clinical microexpressions (1969) and co-developed the 44-Action-Unit Facial Action Coding System growing out of their 1969 nonverbal-leakage framework

people.name: Ernest Haggard & Kenneth Isaacs
people.role: Researchers who first spotted 'micromomentary expressions' (1966) during slow-motion psychotherapy film review

core_facts.fact: In 1969 at UC San Francisco, Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen analyzed 16mm clinical interview films frame by frame at 24 frames per second after a hospitalized patient ('Mary') later confessed she had been hiding acute despair behind a cheerful smile to win a weekend pass.

Played at normal speed, Mary looked convincingly upbeat; stepped frame by frame, a two-frame (1/12-second) flash of intense anguish broke across her brow and mouth before a polite social smile snapped over it.

Building on Haggard & Isaacs (1966), Ekman and Friesen termed these involuntary flashes 'microexpressions' — brief emotional leaks lasting roughly 40 to 200 milliseconds (1/25 to 1/5 of a second) when someone tries to conceal strong affect.

To measure faces objectively without guesswork, Ekman and Friesen spent eight years dissecting facial anatomy to build the Facial Action Coding System (FACS, 1976-1978), cataloging 44 distinct muscular Action Units (e.g., AU6 orbicularis oculi cheek-raiser + AU12 lip-corner puller in a genuine Duchenne smile).

Dual motor wiring explains the leak: voluntary polite smiles travel from motor cortex, whereas urgent emotional expressions fire automatically from subcortical limbic/amygdala-brainstem nuclei milliseconds before cortical suppression catches up.

Crucially, Ekman himself coined 'Othello's Error': spotting a 100-millisecond flash of fear on an innocent suspect's face does NOT prove lying — an honest person terrified of being disbelieved flashes the exact same fear as a guilty liar terrified of getting caught.

Empirical high-stakes courtroom and laboratory studies by Stephen Porter & Leanne ten Brinke (2008) confirmed complete full-face microexpressions are actually rare (appearing in only ~2% of expressions, mostly partial upper- or lower-face leaks) and untrained human lie-detection accuracy averages just 54 percent — barely above a 50/50 toss.

Cross-cultural field studies with isolated Fore communities in Papua New Guinea (Ekman & Friesen, 1971) showed shared recognition of core macro-expressions (anger, fear, disgust, sadness, enjoyment) while cultural 'display rules' govern when people mask them in public.

Slow-motion 24-fps film inspection (isolating 1-to-2-frame leaks around frame 14 on a tabletop Steenbeck viewer) inspired Ekman's microexpression model, though Porter and ten Brinke (2008) found full-face leaks (<1/10 to 1/5 second) in only ~2% of trials.

wow_facts.fact: At normal 24-frames-per-second playback, seasoned psychiatrists saw only a calm smile — stepping the 16mm projector frame by frame exposed a 2-frame (83-millisecond) flash of agony hidden in plain sight.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Slow-motion film revealed a tug-of-war between two separate facial motor systems.

wow_facts.fact: Paul Ekman named psychology's deadliest lie-detection trap after Shakespeare's Othello: Othello saw genuine fear on Desdemona's face and murdered her assuming fear meant guilt — when she was terrified of not being believed.
wow_facts.why_surprising: A microexpression reads hidden EMOTION, never a Pinocchio lie.

wow_facts.fact: Across hundreds of studies (Bond & DePaulo 2006), police, judges, and customs officers spot lies from demeanor at roughly 54 percent accuracy — virtually a 50/50 guess.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Pop-TV 'human lie detector' infallibility is pure fiction.

wow_facts.fact: Ekman and Friesen personally stimulated and photographed every single muscle fiber in their own faces for eight years to map 44 objective Action Units — later adopted by Pixar animators to bring Toy Story and Inside Out faces to life.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Clinical anatomy became the language of modern digital cinema.

misconceptions.myth: There is a 'Pinocchio nose' facial tic or eye-direction tell ('looking up-left = lying') that proves deception 100% of the time.
misconceptions.truth: Zero universal Pinocchio tells exist; eye-gaze direction myths fail completely under controlled testing, and microexpressions show concealed emotion rather than deception.

misconceptions.myth: Liars flash full-face microexpressions every few seconds like TV crime dramas.
misconceptions.truth: Porter & ten Brinke (2008) showed partial upper- or lower-face leakage is far commoner and full-face microexpressions appear on only ~2% of emotional trials.

misconceptions.myth: You can force a completely convincing 'genuine' eye-crinkling smile on command whenever stressed.
misconceptions.truth: Most adults struggle to voluntarily contract the outer orbicularis oculi (AU6) symmetrically without genuine affect while suppressing brow distress (AU1+4).

misconceptions.myth: Microexpression science justifies airport behavior-screening arrests without hard evidence.
misconceptions.truth: Independent scientific audits criticized TSA's SPOT program because nervousness and fatigue mimic 'deception' cues (Othello's Error).

everyday_hooks: Catching a split-second tighten around a friend's eyes right before they smile and say 'No, really, it's totally fine!'
Stopping yourself from accusing a nervous teenager or job candidate of lying just because their voice trembles under authority ('Othello's Error').
Spotting a polite mouth-only 'Pan-Am smile' (AU12 alone) vs a warm eye-crinkling Duchenne smile (AU6 + AU12).
Asking a gentle open question ('Did something about that timeline worry you?') instead of playing amateur mind-reader.
